item.title: Daily Dose of Data Science How work is organized inside a GPU. A GPU does not tr
item.description:
Daily Dose of Data Science
How work is organized inside a GPU.

A GPU does not treat a large computation as one job. It keeps dividing that job into smaller pieces until thousands of simple operations can run together.

The easiest way to understand this is to follow the work from the program you launch to the arithmetic the chip performs.

1) A kernel creates the full workload.

A kernel is a function meant to run repeatedly across different pieces of data. When you launch one, it creates a grid. The grid represents all the work required for that launch.

2) The grid is divided into thread blocks.

Each block owns one portion of the workload. Its threads stay together on the same streaming multiprocessor, or SM, so they can coordinate and exchange values through fast shared memory.

The GPU schedules blocks independently. This allows blocks from a large grid to spread across many SMs without needing to coordinate with one another.

3) Each block is divided into warps.

A thread is one lane performing the kernel’s instructions on its own data. The hardware collects threads into fixed groups of 32 called warps.

A block containing 256 threads therefore becomes eight warps. These warps are the units the SM actually chooses between during execution.

All 32 threads in a warp receive the same instruction. They perform it together, but on different values. This is where the GPU gets its width.

It also explains why branching can hurt performance. If threads in one warp choose different paths, the GPU must run each path separately while temporarily disabling the threads that took the other one.

4) Warps execute inside an SM.

An SM contains compute units, warp schedulers, registers, and shared memory. It can keep many warps resident at once, even though only some execute during a given clock tick.

When one warp requests data from slower memory and has to wait, the scheduler selects another ready warp. Switching is extremely cheap because every resident warp already has its state stored on the SM.

The GPU does not eliminate memory delays. It hides them by always having another warp ready to run.

This hierarchy also explains why workload size matters. Too few blocks leave SMs unused. Too few resident warps leave the scheduler with nothing to execute during a memory stall.

The complete path is simple.

A kernel creates a grid → The grid contains blocks → Blocks contain warps → Warps contain 32 threads → Blocks are assigned to SMs → Their warps are scheduled onto compute units.

That structure is the foundation behind GPU parallelism, latency hiding, and the need for large batches of similar work.

We wrote the full breakdown on how GPUs work, why they are organized this way, and what that design means for LLM performance.

The article is quoted below.

item.title: Akshay 🚀 I have been fine-tuning LLMs for over 3 years now! Here’s how to train
item.description:
Akshay 🚀
I have been fine-tuning LLMs for over 3 years now!

Here’s how to train an LLM on tasks with multiple correct answers:

Consider a model that generates staff schedules.

Two schedules can look completely different while still being valid.

Both may cover every shift, respect employee availability, satisfy labor rules, and remain within budget.

There is no single completion that SFT should teach the model to imitate. What we do have is a set of rules that every valid schedule must satisfy.

This makes the problem a good fit for RLVR.

Amazon SageMaker AI supports this through its serverless model customization workflow and the new Training Sessions APIs.

Training Sessions keep the model loaded in a stateful GPU session while the engineer controls the RL loop, including rollout generation, reward computation, and policy updates.

SageMaker AI manages the underlying GPU infrastructure and distributed execution. The remaining challenge is converting the scheduling requirements into a verifier.

For example:

1. Is every shift covered?
2. Is anyone double-booked?
3. Are all labor rules satisfied?
4. Is the total cost within budget?

Inside this RL loop, the model generates several candidate schedules for each prompt.

The verifier runs the same four checks against every candidate.

For instance, a schedule passing all four checks can receive 1.0, passing three can return 0.75, and so on.

GRPO compares the rewards within each group and updates the model toward the higher-scoring schedules.

The model is therefore not learning one predefined schedule, but instead it is learning to produce schedules that satisfy the underlying specification.

The reward function still needs careful design.

An uncovered shift is not equivalent to exceeding the preferred cost by 1%.

A production verifier should treat coverage, double-booking, and labor rules as hard constraints. Any violation could return zero.

Cost and employee preferences can then act as soft constraints that rank the schedules that remain valid.

This distinction determines what the model eventually optimizes. SageMaker AI manages the customization job, but the verifier remains an engineering and product decision.

If you want to get hands-on and learn more about serverless model customization, AWS has published an interactive workshop: https://t.co/kpNAzwDtAj

SageMaker AI agent skills can also help with model selection, data preparation, job configuration, evaluation, and deployment using Claude Code, Codex, Kiro, or another compatible coding agent.

Moreover, my co-founder also wrote a complete engineering walkthrough of an RLVR experiment on SageMaker AI. I’m quoting his full tutorial below.

Thanks to AWS for collaborating with us on this post.

https://t.co/ZeGyXq8bZT - Avi Chawla

item.title: anshuman RT @RitvikRastogi19 : this can change the way decision models are train
item.description:
anshuman
RT @RitvikRastogi19: this can change the way decision models are trained...

lately, we've seen a growing number of decision models emerge, each with its own architecture, decision head, and training recipe. more recently, Unsloth integrated Clef's architecture into its library, which further intrigued me and prompted me to take a deeper dive into this space.

as i explored the architecture, i felt there was considerable room for simplification. this led me to start experimenting, eventually turning into a controlled study where I fixed the backbone, training data, and training recipe to isolate the impact of individual design choices.

in this paper, i systematically ablate several design decisions:
- effect of decision heads
- effect of scale of the backbone
- effect of post training of the backbone

would love to hear your thoughts!

paper: https://t.co/OdhL6aYGSQ
tweet
